query: For nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts used in ethanol oxidation, strong reported performance has not yet yielded a comprehensive causal understanding of catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability under reaction conditions. Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs one of these behaviors and why. Specify an unnamed controlled change and an appropriate baseline, the predicted observations relative to that baseline, the operating boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The catalytic activity of nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts in ethanol oxidation is governed by the oxidation state of the catalyst components, which can be monitored in real-time using X-ray absorption spectroscopy.
generation.intervention: in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy monitoring of catalyst components during ethanol oxidation

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if no correlation is observed between oxidation state of catalyst components and catalytic activity or durability, the hypothesis is falsified, with a threshold of R^2 < 0.5

To summarize, the mechanisms of high-temperature oxidation in CrMnFeCoNi system reported in references [,,,] were mainly based upon surface analysis of the reaction products retained after tests, which is insufficient because great emphasis has been placed on post-mortem analyses of reaction products analysed at ambient temperature, or else assumptions made via the analysis of the temperature dependence of phases at different temperatures. Clearly, this introduces a degree of uncertainty, since one cannot be completely sure of the underlying physical mechanisms which are imperative on the critical scales: that of the activity of elements, transformation temperatures, and vapour pressure at the same time. Time–temperature-resolved in situ XRD observations would be invaluable in circumventing this ambiguity and in elucidating the chemical processes giving rise to the oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi alloy.

If considering oxides that form at a higher temperature such as 950, 1000, and 1050 °C, the ThermoCalc-predicted spinel oxide type is the same as the experimentally found spinel oxide. The electrochemical activity of HEO‐Air and HEO‐Vac electrocatalysts were analyzed with Rotating Disc Electrode (RDE, BASI) by using a GAMRY Reference 3000 potentiostat/galvanostat/ ZRA. The standard three‐electrode system with platinum wire as a counter electrode, Ag/AgCl as a reference electrode, and glassy carbon electrode (GCE) as a working electrode was used. The catalysts inks were prepared using 5 mg Super‐P carbon, 8 mg of HEO, 50 µL Nafion solution (Sigma–Aldrich, 5 wt.%), and 2 mL ethanol. Ten microliters of catalyst ink was dropped on a GCE and dried in air. The dried electrodes were tested in 0.1 m KOH solution which was saturated with O2 prior to and during the electrochemical tests. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) test was applied between 0.2 and 1.1 V versus Ag/AgCl with a 10 mV s−1 scan rate. All the potentials that are recorded versus Ag/AgCl were normalized to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) according to the Nernst equation.
